card.hook: Hakata Station never stands still: trains slide in, crowds pour out, and the glass and stone glow as the evening comes on. The trick is to get above it all for a calmer look.
card.stand_here: Head up to the rooftop garden 東7番街屋上庭園 in the station area and face the station district, so the lit, Hakata-coloured wall sits in front of you. If you want a wider view with trains below, the rooftop square つばめの杜ひろば is a good second spot.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the lit wall and the rooftops behind it into one layered picture. Then go to 1x for the wider streets, and save 0.5x for close-up details, since it can make buildings lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the line of rooftops on the top third, then tap the lit wall and slide it a little darker so the lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Come in late afternoon and stay into the evening, when the building's lights are on and the sky still has some colour. After dark, switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: On the plaza in front of the west-side Hakata Exit facade, use the front camera and stand so the building fills the frame behind you. Up on the tiered rooftop terrace at Tsubame no Mori Hiroba, try 0.5x to fit more of the view in with you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand back on the open ground in front of the west-side Hakata Entrance, far enough away to fit as much of the building as possible behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Rooftop areas and station facilities can have set opening times and entry rules, so check the official site before you go, including which floor the rooftop is on. Keep other people's faces out of close-ups.
card.challenge: Get a train in the background below you and the glowing wall in the same frame, then see if you can count how many people are in it.
card.good_to_know: The JR Hakata City complex opened on 3 March 2011, and the Kyushu Shinkansen services began nine days later. The very first station here opened in 1889, about 600 m north of where it stands today. On average, 125,462 people boarded here each day in the last full fiscal year.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the rooftop garden 東7番街屋上庭園 in the station area and face the station district, so the lit, Hakata-coloured wall sits in front of you. If you want a wider view with trains below, the rooftop square つばめの杜ひろば is a good second spot.

The 'in front of the Hakata Entrance' location is inferred from a Wikimedia Commons file name only; no page confirms how much of the building fits in a photo from there. For the rooftop terrace, the sources describe the view but do not say the station is directly behind a visitor facing the city, so that framing is unconfirmed. The sources disagree on the floor: one says Amu Plaza's 11th-floor rooftop, another says the 10th floor via the elevators, so check the floor before going. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules at this station, and no safety point was found for it.

card.hook: Picture a shopping centre where a canal runs right through the middle and nobody told the buildings about straight lines. Canal City is so curvy and self-contained that your photos can look like a stage set.
card.stand_here: Start near 祇園町２６８３号線, at the phone icon about 160 m south of the numbered pin, and face north. It's roughly 3 minutes on foot from there to the complex itself.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole scene in. Then try 0.5x to fit in the sweep of the curving buildings and the canal. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out sculptures, signs and fountain details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up the canal or a curved building edge along one line, and add a few people walking past for scale.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening is lovely, when the lights come on and play against the water. Daytime is better if you want clean views of the shapes without lots of lights competing.
card.selfie_here: Head to the railing on the B1 level at the base of the central fountain pool in Sun Plaza. Use your front camera, try 0.5x, and let the fountain sit behind you. The exact spot isn't a marked photo point, so have a quick look around when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: A passer-by on the third-floor balcony above Sun Plaza, by the United Cinemas entrance, could shoot down toward you at the B1 fountain railing. That's a suggestion rather than a marked photo spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed during the fountain show, but don't block other visitors' views. Keep to the open walkways and don't get in the way of shoppers. Fountain times change, so check the posted schedule on site or the official site.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a curve, the water and at least one stranger's umbrella or shopping bag all fit in one frame, and call it your best 'city within a city' shot.
card.good_to_know: Canal City opened on 20 April 1996 and cost about $1.4 billion, the largest private development in Japan's history. The Jerde Partnership designed it in that fanciful, curvy style. The Ramen Stadium arrived in 2001, and for the 20th anniversary in 2016 it added the Aqua Panorama fountain and Japan's largest 3D projection mapping.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near 祇園町２６８３号線, at the phone icon about 160 m south of the numbered pin, and face north. It's roughly 3 minutes on foot from there to the complex itself.

No page explicitly recommends a passer-by position for photographing a visitor with the whole complex; the balcony spot is inferred from pages that recommend it for clean fountain views, so treat it as a suggestion. Viewing advice also conflicts: one guide says to skip the ground-level railing, while another says to claim a B1 railing spot on weekends. card.hook: Picture a red-and-green pavilion standing over still water, its twin reflected below and the city skyline peeking out behind the trees. That's Ōhori Park's Ukimido, and it might be the easiest good-looking photo in Fukuoka.
card.stand_here: Stand on the central island right in front of 浮見堂 (Ukimido), the red-and-green pavilion. You reach it by crossing the bridges, so the walk is part of the fun. Face the pavilion with the lake around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the pavilion and its reflection. Tap 0.5x on the bridges to fit the whole lake and sky in, or 2x to pick out the pavilion from across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a line, keep the pavilion off-centre and let the reflection fill the bottom of the frame, then tap the pavilion and slide a little darker so the red stays rich.
card.best_time: Morning is best, when the water is calmest (that's one guide's advice). Dusk is the moody option, when the lake turns blue and the park lights come on. In that case, use night mode and rest your phone against a railing.
card.selfie_here: Try the Matsushima-bashi bridge, the second bridge from the east. Stand on its western part with the pavilion behind you, use the front camera at 0.5x and let the pavilion sit over your shoulder. One guide suggests arriving about 40 minutes before sunset, and that timing is for late October through February.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to step back from the pavilion to get some distance (one blogger found it looks better from afar) while you stand in front of it on the island.
card.rules_and_safety: The path around the lake is busy with walkers, joggers and dogs, so wait for a gap before you shoot. On rainy days fallen leaves get wet and slippery, so walk carefully and wear waterproof shoes.
card.challenge: Get the pavilion's reflection to fill the bottom of your frame, then hold the phone low to the water and see if you can make the reflection look even better.
card.good_to_know: Ōhori means "large moat". The lake began as part of the moat for Fukuoka Castle, made by the lord Kuroda Nagamasa from the northern half of an old inlet. The park, modelled on the West Lake of China, opened in 1929, and a fireworks festival is held here every August.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the central island right in front of 浮見堂 (Ukimido), the red-and-green pavilion. You reach it by crossing the bridges, so the walk is part of the fun. Face the pavilion with the lake around it.

card.hook: There's a giant festival float parked in the middle of a shrine, and honestly it's hard to walk past without grinning. Kushida Shrine in Fukuoka has bold shapes everywhere: a big torii, a sweeping roof and an old ginkgo with a rope around its trunk.
card.stand_here: The shrine lies to the east, about 40 minutes on foot, so follow the walk on your map app. Once you're at Kushida Shrine, stand on the approach and face the main torii, with the main hall roof rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x on the approach. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the hall roof or the roped ginkgo trunk. Use 0.5x only if you can stand far enough back to keep the torii upright.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the torii posts up with the vertical lines, then tilt your phone up so the torii and roof sit together in one frame.
card.best_time: A weekday is much calmer than a weekend midday, when it gets crowded. Come in late November and the ground under the ginkgo is covered in yellow leaves.
card.selfie_here: Walk round to the back side of the Yamakasa float, away from its showy front. One page calls it the best free photo spot on the grounds, and it's easy to miss. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the float over your shoulder. The short red torii tunnel at the Inari shrine at the back of the grounds is another popular photo spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand in the outer lane in front of the two-storied tower gate (not the central lane, which is reserved for the divine) and frame you with the gate and the main hall roof behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is restricted inside the main hall and in the lucky-charm and ema areas, so follow any signs. Keep your flash off near the main hall, and never aim your phone at people who are praying. The ground can get slippery on drizzly days, so watch your step.
card.challenge: Can you get the torii and the hall roof perfectly stacked in one shot without a single person's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: Kushida Shrine is dedicated to Amaterasu and Susanoo, and it's said to have been founded in 757. It's the centre of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival, which is why the giant float is here. The float is on show year-round except June, though its position in the grounds may change.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The shrine lies to the east, about 40 minutes on foot, so follow the walk on your map app. Once you're at Kushida Shrine, stand on the approach and face the main torii, with the main hall roof rising behind it.

card.hook: Fukuoka Tower is a giant mirror stuck in the sand, so it never looks the same twice. On a hazy day it's pale and silvery, and on a clear day it turns deep blue.
card.stand_here: Head to Momochi Seaside Park (シーサイドももち海浜公園) and stand on the beach, on the ocean side. Face the tower and pick a spot where nothing blocks its base, so you get sand, sea and sky in the same shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower and a good slice of sky. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, or try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a close-up of the mirrored surface.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the phone upright, switch on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line, then tap the sky and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset gives the mirrors lots of sky colour to reflect, but it's also when the tower is busiest. A clear day gives the cleanest, bluest reflection.
card.selfie_here: A visitor review mentions an outdoor photo spot at the front of the tower with a phone holder, so you can fit the whole building behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the tower over your shoulder. Reviews disagree on exactly where that spot is, so have a look around.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the beach in Momochi Seaside Park facing the tower, while you stand where the tower rises behind you, and ask them to hold the phone upright.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower grounds and observation decks may have set visiting rules or ticketing, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the tower now and another later in the day, then see how differently the mirrors have dressed up.
card.good_to_know: Fukuoka Tower is 234 metres tall and the tallest seaside tower in Japan. It was finished in 1989 after 14 months of building, on land reclaimed from Hakata Bay. About 8000 half-mirrors cover its triangular body, which is why it's nicknamed the "Mirror Sail".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Momochi Seaside Park (シーサイドももち海浜公園) and stand on the beach, on the ocean side. Face the tower and pick a spot where nothing blocks its base, so you get sand, sea and sky in the same shot.

card.hook: Picture a bright vermilion pagoda, and then a row of office towers peeking over its shoulder. That's Tōchō-ji: a five-storey wooden showpiece with the city crowding in behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the temple grounds in Hakata, facing the pagoda, then shuffle a few steps to one side until the tower blocks drop out of the frame and only sky and trees sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from a little way back so you get the whole pagoda against the sky. If you're close, switch to 0.5x to fit its full height in. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda and leave the city buildings out.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pagoda, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays blue and the vermilion doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Cherry trees around the pagoda are popular in season, so check the bloom before you go if that's your thing.
card.selfie_here: Head to the back side of the five-storey pagoda, within the temple grounds. One guide points visitors there for the best shots, with the red tower and the trees framing you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the pagoda over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your commemorative shot with you in front of the pagoda, and ask them to frame it so the city buildings behind stay out of the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed inside the Great Buddha hall or the main hall, so keep your shots outdoors. The passage under the Great Buddha is pitch dark, so feel your way along the handrail, and don't use flash or a flashlight there.
card.challenge: Can you find the exact spot where the skyscrapers vanish and the pagoda gets only sky and trees behind it? Bonus points for the temple gate framing it from the street side.
card.good_to_know: Tradition says Kūkai founded Tōchō-ji in 806, which makes it the oldest Shingon temple on Kyushu. It first stood by the sea, and after a fire at the end of the 16th century, Kuroda Tadayuki moved it to its present site. Look out for the hexagonal Rokkaku-dō hall, built in 1842, and the 10.8 metre seated Buddha, carved between 1988 and about 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the temple grounds in Hakata, facing the pagoda, then shuffle a few steps to one side until the tower blocks drop out of the frame and only sky and trees sit behind it.

card.hook: Forget hunting for the one famous angle at Fukuoka Castle. The whole place is a giant stone playground, with huge dry-stone walls, old gates and turrets (yaguras) scattered around Maizuru Park, so you get to pick your own frame.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject in Maizuru Park, below the stone wall. Look up at the turret standing on its high wall, with the rampart framing it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for walls, gates and turrets. Switch to 0.5x when you're close to a long stretch of stonework or want the sky in, but only if you have room to step back, because the edges get stretched. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out turret details or the pattern of the stones.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the base of a wall on the lower line so it leads the eye up to a gate or turret, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the texture of the stone and avoids harsh shadows. Quieter times of day also make it easier to get shots without strangers in them.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera (0.5x if you want more in) in the Shioubu garden beside the Tamon Yagura turret, with the turret over your shoulder. Late May to June, when the iris bloom, is the dream moment. In autumn, try the edge of the Shimanohashi moat with the turret and walls behind you, where they can reflect in the water.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by, stand on the lawn at the foot of the stone wall beneath Shiomi Yagura, and ask them to step back for a wide shot with the turret in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One visitor says the paved floor at the ruins is very slippery, and park paths can be uneven, so watch your step while you look at the screen. Some facilities inside the park may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three versions of one wall: a wide shot, a closer one, and one with you standing by the stones to show how big they are.
card.good_to_know: The castle was finished in 1607 after seven years of building, and it's said to have had 47 yaguras. Its other name, Seki-jō, means 'Stone Castle', which the walls explain nicely. The Minamimaru Tamon Yagura turret dates from 1854 and is an Important Cultural Property.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject in Maizuru Park, below the stone wall. Look up at the turret standing on its high wall, with the rampart framing it.

The Wanderlog review that mentions the slippery floor is a single user comment.

card.hook: After dark, Nakasu looks like someone plugged in an island: neon signs and yatai food stall lights spill right onto the river. The best seat for it is a bridge.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Fukuhaku Deai Bridge (福博であい橋) and look across the Naka River at Nakasu's neon and yatai lights, with the bridge's own lighting framing the view. Nakasu's main area lies to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bridge, the river and the reflections. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want more of the lit-up riverbank, and keep the horizon level so the buildings don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on night mode, brace your elbows on the railing, tap a bright sign, then slide it a little darker so the neon doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the lights are on. The bridge lighting is seasonal, with a winter period of roughly November 2026 to January 2027, so check the dates before you plan your evening.
card.selfie_here: Get your selfie on the bridge deck, using the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the Nakasu glow over your shoulder. For a livelier shot, stand in front of the row of yatai stalls on the riverside walk near Seiryu Park, with the stall street behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the riverside path on the opposite side of the Naka River and shoot straight at the bridge while you stand on the deck, so you appear with the bridge and its night reflection.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask the vendors before photographing the yatai stalls, especially their food, and be mindful of private establishments. Take your time on the bridge and keep out of the way of people walking past.
card.challenge: Find the neon sign that looks best wobbling in the water and make it the star of your photo.
card.good_to_know: Nakasu is a narrow island between the Naka River and the Hakata River, and its name roughly means "the island in the middle". Kuroda Nagamasa, the local lord, created it around 1600 and joined the two sides of the city with bridges. Today it has 18 bridges and is a busy entertainment district, said to have about 3,500 restaurants and shops.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Fukuhaku Deai Bridge (福博であい橋) and look across the Naka River at Nakasu's neon and yatai lights, with the bridge's own lighting framing the view. Nakasu's main area lies to the north.

card.hook: Squint at Acros Fukuoka from across the lawn and the office block turns into a tree-covered hill that's wandered into the middle of Tenjin. That's the whole trick, and it works.
card.stand_here: Stand in Tenjin Central Park (天神中央公園), on the south side, and face north across the lawn toward the building. You'll see the whole stepped, green facade rising over the lawn and trees, with sky above it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the terraces, lawn and sky in one shot. If the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the planters and vines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the terraces up with the horizontal lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the planting looks properly green and the terraces show clearly. A clear sky behind the building makes the outline stand out.
card.selfie_here: Climb to a mid-level terrace of the Step Garden, where the greenery hides the building's edges and gives you a leafy backdrop. Use the front camera, hold it a little below eye level and let the plants fill in behind you. If your front camera has a 0.5x button, it fits more green in.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the park lawn directly in front of the building and ask your helper to stand back on the south side of the park, facing north, so the terraced garden fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Smoking is prohibited in the park, including the rooftop observation deck. Pets aren't allowed on the Step Garden path, though they're fine in Tenjin Central Park. Access to the garden and observation areas can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a strip of lawn and a few trees along the bottom, then try to find the exact spot where the building looks most like a hill.
card.good_to_know: Acros Fukuoka is in the Tenjin district of central Fukuoka, facing Tenjin Central Park on the park's north side. The park is public and free to enter. The building's garden and observation areas may have their own access rules.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Tenjin Central Park (天神中央公園), on the south side, and face north across the lawn toward the building. You'll see the whole stepped, green facade rising over the lawn and trees, with sky above it.

card.hook: Picture a giant silver shell parked behind a sandy beach: that's the dome from the sea side, and it feels more like a seaside postcard than a baseball stadium.
card.stand_here: Stand on the beach side of シーサイドももち海浜公園 (Seaside Momochi Beach Park) and face east, looking at the dome across the sand. The curved roof rises behind the beach and promenade, with Hakata Bay open around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole roof, the beach and the bay. Then try 1x for a calmer view, and 2x or higher if your phone has it, to make the dome look bigger behind the sand.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line so sand or promenade fills the bottom third, then tap the roof and drag the brightness a bit darker if the sky is bright so the pale roof keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon should be lovely, because the sun is behind you in the west and lights the side of the dome facing the beach. Around dusk, switch on night mode for the glowing sky and lights, and hold your phone steady against your body or a rail.
card.selfie_here: Try the bronze hand casts of famous performers along the stadium's outer edge (the Michael Jackson hand is one), or the Hawks Minna no Garden beside Gate 7. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and step back so the dome sits over your shoulder if it fits. Both are known photo spots, but I can't promise the dome will be in the background, so check your screen before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Try the footbridge linking Gate 5 of the dome to MARK IS Fukuoka Momochi, and ask a passer-by to take your photo there.
card.rules_and_safety: Outside access can change on game and event days, so check the official site and the Hawks schedule before you go. Selfie sticks are often banned inside the dome, but that's for the interior, not the outdoor spots.
card.challenge: Keep the sea edge dead straight and wait for someone to stroll along the promenade, so your dome looks properly huge next to a tiny human.
card.good_to_know: The dome is the home ground of the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks and opened in 1993 with about 40,000 seats. It was Japan's first stadium with a retractable roof. The roof is around 12,000 tonnes of steel covered in thin titanium plating, and it's rarely opened, so you'll most likely see it closed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the beach side of シーサイドももち海浜公園 (Seaside Momochi Beach Park) and face east, looking at the dome across the sand. The curved roof rises behind the beach and promenade, with Hakata Bay open around it.

card.hook: Three minutes from a busy subway station, the traffic noise fades and you're under tall trees, looking at old timber gates and tiled roofs. It's a very good plot twist for a Fukuoka afternoon.
card.stand_here: Face north, towards the temple, and walk up to the Sanmon Gate approach to shoot the gate square on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for gates and building fronts, and try 0.5x in the bigger open spaces. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for roof tiles, wooden beams and the bell tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gate, then slide the setting so the picture goes a touch darker, which keeps the pale sky from washing out the dark timber.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter, with softer light and fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone steps of the Butsuden (the Buddhist hall), or stand in front of the Sanmon Gate. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the roofline sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the approach in front of the Sanmon Gate and ask someone to shoot from further back on the path, so the gate fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outdoor grounds are fine for personal use, but not of the interior, and the main hall is closed to visitors. Skip selfie sticks, don't use flash near statues or altars, and ask before photographing any monk. It's also a cemetery, so keep voices down and photograph the buildings, not the graves.
card.challenge: Find one roofline against the sky, turn on gridlines, and get it perfectly level. Bonus points if a tree branch sneaks in as a frame.
card.good_to_know: Shōfuku-ji is described as the oldest Zen temple in Japan. The monk Eisai founded it after returning from China in 1195, and the main buildings went up in the early 1200s. According to temple legend, the Sanmon gate came from Najima Castle, and the Hōjō hall was moved from Hizen Nagoya Castle in 1601. The bell tower dates from 1589.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon: the temple's centre lies 129 m to the north of it, about 2 minutes on foot. Face north, towards the temple, and walk up to the Sanmon Gate approach to shoot the gate square on.

card.hook: Here's a secret: the best photo of an art museum is often the one you take before you go in. Grab a quick shot of the entrance or the sign, and you've got a tidy record of your Fukuoka day.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, where the phone icon on the map sits. Step back as far as feels comfortable and safe, and face the frontage so you can fit more of it in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the entrance. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x to fit the whole building in. Save zoom 2x for signs and banners.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with them so the walls look straight, with any signs in the top or bottom third.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime when the light is soft and even. You get fewer harsh shadows on the front of the building.
card.selfie_here: Head to the big Bu Hua mural (4 x 9 m) on the 1st floor of the Hakata Riverain entrance hall, right in front of the lift to the museum. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more colour, and keep the mural over your shoulder. It's described as a popular photo spot, but we can't promise the museum shows up behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks, video recording and flash aren't allowed at the museum. Personal photos are only okay in some collection areas, and only where signs don't say no, so check the signs or ask staff before you shoot any artworks.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole entrance, then one close-up of a sign or poster, and see if the pair looks like a mini photo story.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1999 and shows modern and contemporary Asian art. It holds about three thousand works from twenty-three countries, mostly from donations and gifts. It grew out of the earlier Fukuoka Art Museum, which ran an Asian art show every five years from 1979 to 1994.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, where the phone icon on the map sits. Step back as far as feels comfortable and safe, and face the frontage so you can fit more of it in.

card.hook: Stand right at the foot of Hakata Port Tower and try to get all 103 metres into your photo. Go on, I'll wait. It's a slim, open-framed tower that looks great against sea and sky, but it needs some room.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits at the tower itself, on the Hakata Port waterfront in Hakata-ku. Once you arrive, step back along the waterfront until the whole tower fits, then face it with the harbour in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close and tilt the phone upwards. Move back to zoom 1x for a calmer, more even view. If your phone has zoom 2x-5x, use it to pick out the top of the tower or the observation level.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon into sunset, when the tower's night lighting begins. You get a softer sky and a lit-up tower in one go. Once the lights are on, try night mode and rest your phone against a rail or wall.
card.selfie_here: Try the waterfront deck just outside the tower's base at Bayside Place Hakata, with the tower behind you. For another backdrop, use the walkway leading up to the tower inside Bayside Place. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you want more tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Hakata Port quay at Bayside Place Hakata Wharf and shoot toward the tower, while you stand in the frame with the tower rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you fancy going up the tower, opening times and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole tower straight on the gridlines with a strip of harbour water along the bottom, so your photo says 'Fukuoka port' and not just 'tall tower'.
card.good_to_know: Hakata Port Tower is 103 metres tall and was built in 1964. Its observation deck sits at 73.5 metres. The tower is in Hakata-ku, Fukuoka, on the Hakata harbour waterfront.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits at the tower itself, on the Hakata Port waterfront in Hakata-ku. Once you arrive, step back along the waterfront until the whole tower fits, then face it with the harbour in the frame.

card.hook: Picture one long, straight path with the tower gate and main hall lined up at the end of it, like they're queuing for your photo. That's the approach at Hakozaki Shrine, and it's a lovely thing to walk down.
card.stand_here: Stand on the approach and face the tower gate and main hall, so both sit together in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the approach, tower gate and main hall in together. Drop to 0.5x only if crowds or a tight spot stop you fitting it all in. Use zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a closer shot of the tower gate and its roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tower gate on the central line, and let the approach lead the eye to it. Hold the phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, with softer light. Festival days (3 January and 12 to 18 September) draw big crowds, so avoid them for a clear view of the approach, or give yourself extra time.
card.selfie_here: Head down to Oshioi Beach (お潮井浜), the beach in front of the shrine. Stand on the sand with the shrine grounds behind you, use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if you want more of the scene over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the entrance end of the approach and shoot toward the tower gate, with you a bit further along in front of it. The old first torii gate is gone, so don't expect it in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship. Please don't photograph inside the main hall or during ceremonies. Drones and commercial shoots aren't allowed on the grounds, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower gate and main hall sitting in the middle third of your frame with the buildings dead straight, then swap in a portrait of a friend against the long vermilion fence.
card.good_to_know: Hakozaki Shrine is one of Fukuoka's most important Shintō shrines, dedicated to the kami Hachiman, and it was founded in 923. It burned down during the Mongol invasion of 1274. When it was rebuilt, the tower gate got a calligraphy panel reading Tekikoku kōfuku, meaning 'surrender of the enemy nation'. The main hall, worship hall and tower gate are all listed as important cultural assets of Japan.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The shrine is about 28 m to the south-west of the phone icon, which is under a minute on foot. Stand on the approach and face the tower gate and main hall, so both sit together in one frame.

selfie_spots.why: The official shrine site says both the grounds set against the Oshioi and the Oshioi set against the grounds give spectacular views.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot could be sourced with the landmark behind the visitor; the second candidate (the torii on the shore at Hakozaki beach, seen from the grounds) is a scenic view, not a selfie position, so I left it out. The 'you in front of the gate' placement for the ask-someone spot is my inference; the official page only confirms the framing. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules, so none are listed. A travel listing says photography is prohibited in the main area during ceremonies, but that is a general photo rule, not a selfie or tripod rule, so I did not include it. Do not confuse this with the Hakozaki Hachiman Shrine in Izumi, Kagoshima, which has a similar name and a giant bell; the Tripadvisor photos for that shrine are not relevant here. The coordinates you gave (33.61444, 130.42333) fall in Fukuoka's Higashi Ward, matching the Fukuoka shrine.

card.hook: Here's a nice surprise: you don't have to go inside Jōten-ji to get a picture that feels properly Zen. The stone-paved lane, the trees and the temple roofs do all the work from the street.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stone-paved lane, 承天寺通り (Jōtenji-dori), beside the temple, and look north along it. The temple buildings and the white-gravel sand garden sit at a distance, with trees framing the scene.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lane, temple and trees together. If the lane feels too narrow, try 0.5x, then zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the gravel garden and roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the lane in the lower third of the frame, then tap the temple buildings and slide it a little darker if the white gravel looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be calmer. In the evening the area can get busy during the Hakata light-up walk, so be patient and wait for gaps in the crowd. At night, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone paving just past the Hakata Sennen Gate, on the path that runs through the gate toward the temple. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the lane and the greenery fit behind your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed which way works best here, so take a few and see which one you like.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the roadway opposite the wooden sanmon gate while you stand at the granite steps in front of it, so the gate is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the grounds, but some areas are restricted, so follow any signs. Skip restricted areas and religious ceremonies, and check the official site before you go in, as the grounds and sand garden may be ticketed.
card.challenge: Walk back to the Hakata Sennen Gate and find the peach-shaped ornaments on its roof tiles. Can you get one in focus with the path stretching out behind it?
card.good_to_know: The priest Enni-Ben'en founded this Rinzai Zen temple after returning from China, and building work was completed in 1242. He is also credited with bringing the know-how for udon, soba and manjū back to Japan, so it's a fun stop for food fans. The Hakata Sennen Gate by the start of the lane was finished on 28 March 2014. It's a wooden four-legged gate with a tile roof, about 8 metres tall and wide.

Sources give different addresses for the temple (1-29-9 and 1-1-25 Hakata-ekimae/ekiminami), but the coordinates given match the Hakata-ekimae site.
